prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator with Jessica Livingston, and press coverage keeps describing early YC as a one-man show. Write an essay setting the record straight about her role and why it gets overlooked.
response:
**The Other Half of the Y Combinator Story: Why Jessica Livingston’s Name Gets Lost in the Noise**

If you ask the average tech journalist or early-stage founder to describe the founding of Y Combinator in 2005, they will almost invariably give you the same narrative. It is a story of a brilliant, eccentric computer scientist—Paul Graham—who, along with his partner Jessica Livingston, decided to solve the "funding gap" for startups. It is a story of Paul writing essays, building the platform, and pitching to investors. Jessica is there, yes. She is in the photos. She is the co-founder. But in the retelling, she is often relegated to the background, a supportive presence whose primary contribution was… well, being there.

This is not just an oversight; it is a distortion of history.

The reality is that Y Combinator was not a one-man show with a wife in the corner. It was a true partnership between two people who were indispensable to each other. Jessica Livingston was not merely an administrator or a cheerleader. She was the operational engine, the investor relations lead, and the co-architect of the program’s structure. Her role was as critical to YC’s success as Paul’s code and essays, yet it has been systematically overlooked. Why?

### The Invisible Labor of Operations

The most common reason for Jessica’s marginalization is the nature of her work. Paul Graham’s contributions to YC were highly visible and easily quantifiable. He wrote the famous "Do Things That Don’t Scale" essay. He designed the application process. He sat in the demo day presentations. His work produced tangible artifacts: text, code, and public discourse.

Jessica’s work, by contrast, was invisible. She handled the logistics that kept the company running. She negotiated with landlords. She managed the budget. She tracked which startups had filed their paperwork and which hadn’t. She organized the demo days. She fielded the hundreds of emails from applicants and investors. In the tech industry, there is a pervasive bias that values "creation" over "coordination." Writing a brilliant blog post is seen as "real work." Ensuring that the office has internet, that the lawyers are paid, and that the 12 startups in the batch have their cap tables in order is seen as "admin."

This bias is unfair and it is dangerous. A brilliant product without operational execution is a failed company. YC’s value proposition wasn’t just that it taught startups how to grow; it was that it removed the friction of startup formation. Jessica was the one who removed that friction. Without her, Paul would have been spending his time answering email instead of mentoring. The program would have collapsed under the weight of its own bureaucracy.

### The Investor’s Investor

The second reason Jessica’s role is overlooked is that her primary external function was raising money. Paul was the face to the startups; Jessica was the face to the capital. In the early days of YC, the biggest barrier to entry wasn’t finding good startups; it was finding investors who would back them.

Jessica Livingston had spent the previous decade at various VC firms, including Benchmark. She knew the investors. She knew how they thought. She knew what made them say "yes." She was the bridge between the scrappy, unproven YC batch and the deep pockets of Silicon Valley.

When YC announced a batch, it wasn’t just Paul pitching the thesis. It was Jessica leveraging her network to ensure that the demo day wasn’t empty. She was the one who convinced Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, and others to show up. She was the one who made the YC badge a signal of quality to the investment community.

This work is often attributed to the "brand" of YC or to Paul’s reputation. But brands don’t build themselves, and reputations don’t make introductions. Jessica did. She was the chief development officer of the ecosystem. Without her, YC would have been a great school with no customers.

### The Gendered Lens

We cannot ignore the elephant in the room: gender.

When a man and a woman co-found a company, the default assumption in media coverage is that the man is the "visionary" and the woman is the "operator" or the "designer" or the "HR person." This is a trope so common it has its own name: "well, actually, she’s the COO."

Paul Graham was the obvious "tech guy." He wore the t-shirt, he wrote the code, he fit the archetype of the hacker-hero that the tech press loves to tell. Jessica, a lawyer by training and a partner in a VC firm by experience, did not fit that archetype. She was the "business" half. And in the tech press, the "business" half is always less interesting than the "tech" half.

This is not just a matter of who got the headline. It is a matter of who gets the credit. When YC succeeded, the narrative became: "Paul Graham had a great idea." It never became: "Paul and Jessica built a machine." The singular masculine pronoun swallowed the partnership.

### The Record Must Be Straight

Why does this matter? Because it matters for the future.

If we continue to tell the story of Y Combinator as Paul Graham’s solo genius, we reinforce the idea that the most important jobs in tech are the visible, creative, technical ones. We devalue the operational, relational, and financial work that makes those creative jobs possible. We tell the next generation of women in tech that their role will be to support the man who has the idea, rather than to be the one who makes the idea real.

Jessica Livingston was not a sidekick. She was a co-founder. She brought the operational discipline, the investor relationships, and the legal expertise that turned a clever blog post into a global institution. She negotiated the terms. She managed the risk. She built the network.

The next time you read an article about the early days of Y Combinator, look for her name. If it’s missing, ask yourself why. It’s not because she wasn’t there. It’s because the story was told by people who only see what looks like code, and not what looks like work.

The record needs to be straight. Y Combinator was not a one-man show. It was a two-person team. And without Jessica Livingston, there would be no Y Combinator.

prompt: Write a short essay of writing advice: why do people write so differently from how they talk, and what should they do about it?
response:
There is a profound disconnect between the rhythm of our thoughts and the architecture of our sentences. When we speak, we are engaged in a high-bandwidth, low-latency transaction. We rely on context, tone, eye contact, and the immediate feedback loop of the listener to fill in the gaps. Our speech is often elliptical, repetitive, and fragmented. We say, "And so, you know, the thing is, it’s not really the money, it’s the principle," because the listener’s nod confirms we are on the same page.

Writing, however, is a monologue. It is asynchronous and silent. The reader has no access to your furrowed brow or your hand gestures. They cannot ask you to clarify a dangling modifier. If you write exactly as you speak, you produce prose that is often breathless, meandering, and clogged with filler words like "basically," "actually," and "literally." The primary reason people write so differently from how they talk is that they are failing to translate a collaborative performance into a solitary artifact. They are trying to capture the *energy* of the conversation without stripping away the *noise* of the delivery.

So, what should writers do about it? The answer is not to stop sounding like yourself, but to curate who that self is.

First, embrace the draft as a recording. Write the first pass exactly how you would say it out loud. This preserves your voice, your idioms, and your unique cadence. It keeps the text from becoming sterile or overly academic. This is the raw material.

Second, apply the "Silent Partner" test. Read your draft aloud, but imagine you are speaking to someone who is not in the room and cannot hear you. Where do you stumble? Where do you repeat yourself because you expect an interruption? Cut those parts. In writing, you have the luxury of time and revision. You can arrange ideas in a logical sequence rather than the associative order in which they pop into your head.

Finally, recognize that clarity is a form of respect. When we speak, we can rely on charisma to carry a confusing point. When we write, we must rely on structure. A writer’s job is to be the editor of their own impulse. You must take the chaotic, honest stream of consciousness and shape it into a vehicle that can carry meaning across the silence between you and the reader. Do not abandon your voice; just polish it until it shines in the quiet.

prompt: I want an essay for startup founders about the single most important question to ask once a company is several months old: on current revenue growth and expenses, does it reach profitability before the money runs out?
response:
# The Runway Reality Check: The Question Every Founder Must Ask

In the early days of a startup, the air is thick with potential. The narrative is driven by what *could* be: the massive total addressable market, the disruptive technology, the visionary team. Investors fund this narrative, and founders often live inside it, measuring success by user acquisition metrics, press mentions, and the sheer velocity of feature development.

However, there is a specific moment—usually somewhere between month six and month twelve—when the magic of early enthusiasm should give way to the cold, hard arithmetic of survival. At this stage, the most important question a founder can ask is not about market fit, not about competition, and not about the next hire. It is a binary, financial question:

**On current revenue growth and expenses, does the company reach profitability before the money runs out?**

This question is brutal because it rarely has a comforting answer. But it is indispensable because it serves as the ultimate truth serum for a business model.

### The Trap of "Eventually"

Many founders fall into the trap of believing in "eventual" profitability. They assume that if they just scale marketing spend, if they just land one more enterprise deal, or if they just optimize the sales cycle, the unit economics will magically flip positive. They are running a projection where growth is linear or exponential, but costs remain flat or decrease.

This is dangerous. By the time a company is several months old, you no longer have hypotheses; you have data. You know your Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC). You know your churn rate. You know your gross margins. If, when you plot these *actual* figures against your current burn rate, the line never crosses the break-even point before your cash hits zero, you do not have a business problem. You have a funding problem.

There is a critical difference between a company that is temporarily unprofitable while building a moat and a company that is structurally unprofitable. The first can survive a Series A. The second will die in the dilution of a Series B or B+, or worse, in a down round that breaks the equity structure.

### The Math of Survival

To answer this question honestly, you must look at two lines: the revenue line and the expense line.

First, look at your revenue growth. Is it compounding? If you are growing 5% month-over-month, you are not scaling; you are stalling. For the profitability curve to intersect with the runway curve, revenue growth usually needs to be aggressive enough to offset the diminishing returns of scale. If your revenue growth is flat, your path to profitability is a straight line into the ground.

Second, look at your expenses. This is where the ego of the founder is tested. Can you cut costs without killing the engine? If your burn rate is driven by non-essential overhead, you can extend the runway. But if your burn rate is driven by the core cost of serving customers (COGS) and sales efficiency, and those are inefficient, cutting costs is just delaying the inevitable.

The question forces you to calculate the "Time to Break-Even" (TBE) and compare it to your "Cash Runway." If TBE > Runway, you are dead unless you raise money.

### Why This Changes Your Strategy

Once you accept that the answer to this question is likely "no," your entire strategic focus shifts.

If the answer is "no," you stop optimizing for growth at all costs. You start optimizing for efficiency. You stop trying to be the biggest company in the room and start trying to be the most efficient. You look at your CAC payback period. If it takes 18 months to recover the cost of acquiring a customer, and you only have 12 months of runway, you cannot afford to acquire customers at that rate. You must change the product, the pricing, or the sales motion to improve the math.

This question also forces a difficult conversation with your board and investors. You are no longer asking for money to "fuel growth." You are asking for money because the current model does not work. This changes the tone of the negotiation. It moves you from a position of power (I am hot, give me money) to a position of partnership (Here is why the current model is broken, here is how I will fix it, and here is the capital required to execute the fix).

### The Antidote to Hype

The most dangerous thing for a startup is the gap between narrative and reality. Investors and founders often build a story where the company is "on track." But "on track" to what? If the track leads to insolvency, being on track is useless.

Asking "Do we reach profitability before the money runs out?" strips away the hype. It forces you to confront the physical limits of your resources. It reminds you that a startup is not a perpetual motion machine; it is a biological organism that needs food (cash) to grow. If it eats more than it produces, it will starve, no matter how beautiful its ecosystem is.

In the end, profitability is the only metric that matters in the long run. Revenue is vanity; cash flow is sanity; but profitability is viability. If you cannot answer "yes" to that single question, you do not have a company. You have a prototype. And prototypes are meant to be iterated on, not scaled.

prompt: You've spent years picking which early-stage startups to fund. Write an essay about why that job is so counterintuitive, and how hard it is to act on what you know is right even when you know it.
response:
The first thing they don’t tell you about venture capital is that it is not a profession for people who like certainty. It is a profession for people who have made peace with being wrong. But that is a sterile, academic way to describe the psychological toll of the job. In practice, the counterintuitive nature of early-stage investing is not just about risk; it is about the specific, gnawing friction between your intellectual judgment and your emotional self-preservation.

To understand why, you have to understand what you are actually buying. When you write a check for a Series A or even a pre-seed round, you are not buying a product. You are not buying a technology, though the tech may be cool. You are not buying a market, though the market may be large. You are buying a human being. You are buying the founder’s ability to endure the next three years of near-total isolation, the ability to pivot when the data says the pivot is the right move, and the ability to look you in the eye when the metrics are flat and explain why you should keep going.

This is where the counterintuitive trap begins. The human brain is wired to predict outcomes based on visible evidence. If a car engine is running hot, it will likely break. If a stock price has risen steadily for a decade, it is likely to continue rising. This is pattern recognition, and it serves us well in most aspects of life. But in early-stage venture capital, the signal is almost entirely noise, and the noise is often misleading. The most promising companies look like failures. They are messy, their financials are a disaster, their team is arguing, and their customer acquisition costs are higher than their revenue. A seasoned investor knows this. They know that the chaos is the price of admission for high growth. But knowing this intellectually is very different from feeling it in your gut.

The gut, the lizard brain, screams that something is wrong. It sees the red flags and interprets them as danger. It sees the lack of clarity and interprets it as incompetence. So, you are constantly fighting your own biology. You have to look at a company that is on the verge of collapse and see the spark of genius that will save it. You have to ignore the immediate, visceral discomfort of a founder who is difficult, eccentric, or unpolished, because history has shown that the "perfect" founder is often a mediocre operator who cannot handle the pressure of scaling.

This is why the job is so hard. It is not hard because you cannot do the math. The math is simple: you need ten companies to fail to fund one that returns your fund. You need to be wrong seven out of ten times. The problem is that being wrong is painful. It is not a sterile statistic. It is a meeting where you have to tell a founder you are stopping their salary. It is watching a team you liked and respected disintegrate. It is the email in your inbox at 2 AM from a founder who is desperate, and you know that if you don’t answer, they might quit.

The true test of an investor is not whether they pick the winner. Everyone picks a winner eventually. The test is whether they can act on what they know is right when they know it is wrong.

Consider the scenario. You have done the diligence. You have spoken to the customers. You have looked at the code. You have spent hours with the founder, and you have seen the thing. You have seen the obsession. You know, with a level of confidence that feels almost physical, that this person will do what needs to be done. The market is not ready. The team is small. The product is a demo. But you know.

And then you bring it to the investment committee.

The committee is composed of your peers. They are smart. They are cautious. They have survived many winters. They look at the same data you looked at, but they weigh it differently. They see the lack of revenue and they see a lack of validation. They see the high burn rate and they see a lack of discipline. They ask the questions that are hard to answer. They point out the risks that you have already weighed and decided were acceptable.

In that room, you feel the weight of your own track record. You know that if you say yes, and they fail, it is your name on the failure. If you say no, and they fail, you are safe. If you say no, and they succeed, you miss out. But the pain of missing out is a dull ache that fades. The pain of being the one who signed off on a total loss is a sharp, public wound.

So, you argue. You make your case. You talk about the founder’s resilience. You talk about the long-term trajectory. But you can feel the room shifting. You can feel the doubt creeping into your own voice. Did I really see the spark, or did I just want to? Is this conviction, or is it just hope?

And this is the hardest part. You know what is right. You know the thesis holds. But you also know the alternative: being wrong. And the human mind is not built to prioritize long-term expected value over short-term emotional safety. You have to override your instinct to seek safety. You have to choose the path that is more likely to hurt you in the short term because it is more likely to be correct in the long term.

Sometimes, you win the vote. Sometimes, you lose. And sometimes, you lose because you hesitated. You lost because, for a second, you let the fear of being wrong overpower the knowledge of being right. And that is the tragedy of the job. You can be right, and you can still fail. You can be wrong, and you can still succeed. But the only thing you can control is whether you acted in alignment with your best judgment, even when it felt dangerous, even when it felt foolish, even when the world around you was telling you to step back.

This is why I stay in the job. It is not for the money, and it is not for the prestige. It is because there are moments, rare and fleeting, where the fog lifts. You see the shape of the future before it arrives. You see a person who will change something, and you have the power to help them. And in those moments, the counterintuitive nature of the job stops being a burden. It becomes a privilege. You are paid to be wrong. You are paid to see the signal in the noise. And you are paid to have the courage to bet on it, even when you are terrified you are mistaken.

That is the job. It is not investing. It is the practice of acting on conviction in the face of uncertainty. And it is the hardest thing I have ever done.

prompt: You've been running an online discussion community for two years as a side project. Write an essay on what you've learned: about growth, keeping the quality up, bad submissions and bad comments, and the people a site like that attracts.
response:
The first year of running *The Quiet Corner*—my small, text-heavy forum dedicated to analog photography and slow living—felt like managing a garden. You planted seeds, you watered them, and you waited. By the end of that first year, we had 4,000 users. It was intimate. I knew the regulars by their usernames. When a new thread started, I could predict the tone: respectful, curious, slightly melancholic.

Then, in month fourteen, a tech blog linked to us.

Within 48 hours, our user count jumped to 12,000. Within a week, it was 30,000. The garden didn’t just grow; it was bulldozed and paved over with a shopping mall. And that is the first, most painful lesson of running an online community: **Growth is not a metric to be celebrated; it is a threat to be managed.**

For two years, I have learned that the "more is better" ethos of Silicon Valley is antithetical to the health of a niche community. Scale dilutes culture. When I started, the barrier to entry was low but the cultural barrier was high. You had to understand that a grainy film photograph wasn’t "badly taken"; it was a choice. When the influx hit, that nuance evaporated. Suddenly, threads were filled with people asking why their phone photos looked "flat" compared to Instagram filters, or demanding mods remove "low-effort" posts that were actually just honest, unpolished snapshots.

This brings me to the second lesson: **Quality control is not about censorship; it is about curation.**

In the early days, I thought my job as a moderator was to remove spam and trolls. I was wrong. My job was to maintain the signal-to-noise ratio. As the community grew, the "bad submissions" stopped being obvious. They weren’t spam links or hate speech. They were *disconnected* posts. They were users who had no context for why they were there. They posted because they could, not because they had something to add to the specific conversation happening in that corner of the internet.

I tried to fight this with stricter submission rules. "No self-promotion," "No generic questions," "Must include context." It didn’t work. People bypassed it. They posted generic questions in the comments instead. They posted self-promotion in their bios. The rules became a game of whack-a-mole.

The turning point came when I realized that the quality drop wasn’t caused by the new users. It was caused by the old users, who were now overwhelmed. The veterans, the people who built the culture, started to withdraw. They stopped posting. They stopped moderating. They just lurked, or left. And when the people who *get it* leave, the center of gravity shifts toward the loudest, most confused newcomers.

This is where the "bad comments" enter the picture, and this is the most emotionally taxing part of the job.

I used to think bad comments were about content. "This is a bad photo." "You’re wrong." But in a growing community, bad comments are about *status*.

The newcomers didn’t have a reputation to defend. They were free. They could be cruel because anonymity removed the social cost of cruelty. I saw users who had been gentle for months suddenly snap at a new member for misspelling a camera model. I saw users who had never posted a single original thought suddenly become aggressive gatekeepers, policing the grammar of others while their own posts were riddled with errors.

I learned that you cannot mod bad comments. You can delete them, sure, but you cannot delete the *feeling* behind them. The feeling that the community has changed, that the tribe has expanded, and that the new blood is diluting the purity of the group. The bad comments were a symptom of a culture shock, not a cause.

And that leads to the third lesson, the one that still keeps me up at night: **You do not attract the people you want. You attract the people you are.**

I started *The Quiet Corner* because I loved solitude. I loved the idea of a place where people could share their work without the dopamine hit of "likes." I wanted a sanctuary. But I was wrong about what a sanctuary is. A sanctuary is a place you go to hide from the world. But an online community is a world. And people who are lonely, who are angry, who are looking for validation, who are bored, or who are trying to prove they are better than everyone else—they all smell a place where people are gathering. They all smell a place where someone is listening.

The people my site attracts are not just "photography enthusiasts." They are people who are struggling to connect in a way that feels real. They are people who are tired of the performative nature of mainstream social media. But they are also people who are still learning how to behave in a digital space. They are messy. They are contradictory. They want to be seen, but they want to be seen on their own terms.

I have spent two years learning to stop trying to curate a perfect community. A perfect community is a dead community. It has no friction, no growth, no life.

So, what do I do now?

I stopped chasing growth. I stopped caring about the number in the top right corner. I started focusing on the "core." I identified the 500 users who had been here since the beginning. I created a private channel for them. Not to exclude the others, but to give the veterans a place to breathe. To let them talk to each other without the noise.

I also stopped trying to fix the newcomers. I stopped writing long, preachy welcome posts. I started posting short, personal answers. I answered questions directly. I showed up. I reminded people that I was a person, not a bot.

The bad submissions still come. The bad comments still happen. But the signal is coming back. The garden is growing back in. It’s slower now. It’s messier. There are weeds.

But it’s real.

Running an online community for two years has taught me that you are not the architect of a space. You are the host of a party. And a good host doesn’t try to control the guests. They just make sure the music isn’t too loud, the lights aren’t too dim, and that everyone has a drink in their hand. They don’t try to make the party perfect. They just try to keep it going.

And if the party gets too big, if the noise becomes unbearable, you have to make a hard choice. You can let it become a stadium. Or you can close the doors.

I haven’t made that choice yet. But I’m no longer afraid of it.

prompt: Write an essay about how the city you live in shapes your ambitions. Do different cities push people toward different kinds of success, and how should an ambitious young person decide where to live?
response:
**The Architecture of Ambition: How Geography Defines Success**

We often speak of ambition as an internal fire, a personal drive that exists independently of where we plant our feet. However, for those who have moved cities, the illusion of a location-independent self quickly dissolves. The city one lives in does not merely provide a backdrop for one’s career; it acts as a sculptor, chiseling away at what is feasible and reinforcing what is valued. Different urban environments push people toward distinct definitions of success, and for the ambitious young person, choosing a city is not just a logistical decision—it is a strategic alignment of values with infrastructure.

In Silicon Valley, for instance, ambition is often quantified by scale and disruption. The local culture celebrates the "unicorn," the product that changes the world, and the exit that yields billions. Here, success is exponential. If you are not growing at a rate that defies physics, you are stagnating. This environment shapes its residents to be risk-takers, to view failure as a necessary tuition for success, and to prioritize speed over polish. A young engineer living in Palo Alto is likely to define their peak achievement not by job security, but by their ability to leverage leverage—to build a platform that touches millions. The city’s proximity to venture capital, its density of peer innovators, and its cultural narrative of "move fast and break things" create a gravity well that pulls talent toward high-variance, high-reward pursuits.

Conversely, consider Zurich or Vienna. These cities do not reject ambition; rather, they redefine it. In these locations, success is often measured by stability, craftsmanship, and work-life balance. The infrastructure supports long-term thinking: robust social safety nets, efficient public transportation, and a cultural reverence for expertise over hype. A young architect or financial analyst in Zurich is likely to pursue a trajectory of deepening specialization rather than rapid scaling. Ambition here is quiet and durable. It is the ambition to build a legacy that lasts decades, not quarters. The city pushes its inhabitants toward a kind of success that is sustainable, encouraging them to ask, "Is this work meaningful?" rather than "Is this work viral?"

Even within the United States, the contrast is stark. New York City is a machine for prestige and visibility. It rewards the loud, the networked, and the relentless. To be successful in NYC is to be seen. The city’s verticality and density create a competitive pressure that accelerates career progression, often at the cost of personal time. A young professional in Manhattan is likely to define success by title, access, and influence. In contrast, a city like Austin or Portland often fosters a more communal, creative, or entrepreneurial form of ambition. Success there might look like owning a small business with a loyal local following, or creating art that resonates with a specific community. The lower cost of living and the more relaxed pace allow for a different kind of growth—one that is perhaps less about climbing a corporate ladder and more about building a life that feels authentic.

So, how should an ambitious young person decide where to live? The answer lies in diagnosing the specific flavor of ambition they possess.

First, the individual must ask: *What does my ideal day look like?* If the answer involves intense, high-stakes collaboration and the thrill of building something new from scratch, a hub of innovation like San Francisco or London may be the necessary fuel. If the answer involves deep focus, long hours without interruption, and a high quality of life, a quieter, perhaps smaller city might allow for the kind of sustained effort that produces masterful work.

Second, one must consider the *social proof* of their goals. Humans are social creatures who calibrate their behavior against the people around them. If you wish to become a poet, living in a city that only celebrates hedge funds will make your ambition feel like a failure, even if it is succeeding on its own terms. You need an ecosystem that validates your specific definition of success. You need mentors, peers, and a cultural narrative that says, "What you are doing is valuable."

Finally, the decision should account for *timing*. A young person with little capital and high energy might thrive in a chaotic, fast-paced city where opportunities are abundant and the cost of entry is low in terms of social barriers. Later in life, as priorities shift toward family, health, or legacy, a different city may better support the next phase of ambition.

Ultimately, the city is a mirror and a mold. It reflects back to us what is possible and reinforces the habits we need to get there. To choose where to live is to choose which version of oneself one wishes to become. The most ambitious choice is not always the one that offers the highest salary or the most famous zip code; it is the one where the external environment aligns with the internal compass, allowing the individual to pursue their specific definition of success without constant friction.

prompt: Write an essay about being judged: admissions, hiring, investors, dating. Is it right to call it unfair when these decisions go against us, and how should knowing the answer change the way we handle rejection?
response:
**The Lens of Selection: Rethinking Rejection in a Meritocratic Illusion**

In the modern Western narrative, success is frequently framed as a direct correlation between effort and reward. We are taught that if we work hard, if we are talented, and if we are "good people," the doors of opportunity should swing open. When they do not, the immediate emotional reaction is one of violation. We feel judged, scrutinized, and ultimately rejected. This instinct leads us to label these outcomes as "unfair."

However, this framing of life as a series of binary judgments—where we are either accepted or dismissed based on our intrinsic worth—is a fundamental misunderstanding of how social and economic systems actually function. Admissions, hiring, investing, and dating are not moral trials; they are selection processes. Understanding the distinction between being *judged* and being *selected* is crucial, not only for our emotional resilience but for our strategic approach to the world.

To call these rejections "unfair" is to confuse equity with equality, and morality with mechanism. Unfairness implies a breach of rules or a bias that distorts the playing field. While bias exists and is worth fighting, the baseline mechanism of selection is not inherently unfair; it is efficient. A university with 30,000 applicants and 1,000 spots cannot accept everyone who is "good enough." It must rank. An investor with a limited fund size cannot back every promising startup. It must choose. A human being in dating cannot love everyone who finds them attractive. They must select a partner.

The discomfort we feel when we lose these selections often stems from conflating our professional or romantic value with our human dignity. When we are rejected by a hiring manager, it does not mean we are a bad employee; it means we did not fit the specific, narrow needs of that company at that specific moment. When a date does not text back, it does not mean we are unlovable; it means the chemistry or life circumstances did not align. By labeling the outcome as "unfair," we implicitly assume there is a "fair" outcome that was stolen from us by a flawed system. In reality, there is only the outcome that occurred.

Accepting this shift in perspective does not mean we should become passive or accept toxic environments. It means we stop expecting the world to mirror our internal sense of self-worth. If we view rejection as a moral judgment, we will respond with defensiveness, anger, or shame. We will try to argue our case, to prove that the judge was wrong, or we will internalize the verdict. But if we view rejection as a mismatch of variables, our response changes from emotional to analytical.

Knowing that the system is a filter, not a court of law, changes how we handle the "no." It allows us to ask better questions. Instead of asking, "Why didn’t they like me?" (which invites self-doubt), we ask, "What specific criteria did I fail to meet?" Was it a skills gap? A cultural mismatch? A timing issue? In the context of investors and hiring, this is actionable data. In the context of admissions, it is a signal to diversify one’s profile or target different institutions. In the context of dating, it is a prompt to refine one’s understanding of what one actually wants in a partner, rather than simply increasing the volume of applications.

Furthermore, this perspective liberates us from the tyranny of the "perfect candidate." If we believe the system is fair in a moral sense, we feel pressure to be flawless before we present ourselves. We polish the resume to hide gaps, curate the dating profile to hide flaws, and rehearse the interview answer to sound ideal. This is exhausting and often counterproductive because it prevents authenticity. But if we understand that we are competing in a game of optimization, not virtue, we can be more strategic about where we spend our energy. We don’t need to be the best person; we need to be the best fit for this specific container.

There is, of course, a danger in this rationalization. If we view all rejection purely as mechanical, we risk becoming cold or cynical. We might ignore genuine bias or systemic exclusion because we are too busy analyzing our own "marketability." It is important to acknowledge that some rejections *are* unfair—born of racism, sexism, ageism, or nepotism. We must remain vigilant against these. But the key is to identify them for what they are: deviations from the stated rules, not the rules themselves. We fight the bias, but we do not fight the mechanism of selection.

Ultimately, the way we handle rejection is a reflection of our self-concept. If our sense of worth is tethered to external validation, every "no" is a crisis of identity. If our sense of worth is internal and separate from our utility, a "no" is simply information. It tells us where we stand, what we need to improve, or where we need to go next.

We are judged, yes. But we are not defined by those judgments. We are defined by how we iterate. The world will always filter us. The only question is whether we will let that filtering break us, or whether we will use it to refine ourselves into something more precise, more resilient, and more ready for the next opportunity. Fairness is a political ideal; selection is a physical reality. Embracing the latter is the first step toward mastering the former.

prompt: I'd like a light, reflective blog post built around a simple self-test for figuring out what you're actually dependent on in daily life. Use yourself as the example and be honest about what it reveals.
response:
**The Three-Click Test: What We’re Actually Hungry For**

I’ve been trying to be more intentional with my morning. No phone before the coffee. No news before the stretch. It’s a lovely idea, and for about twenty minutes each day, I succeed.

But then, the silence gets loud.

I find myself drifting back to the screen, not because I need information, but because I need *something*. A ping. A scroll. A confirmation that the world is still moving and I am still connected to it.

It made me wonder: if I stripped away the convenience, the entertainment, and the social validation, what is the bare minimum I actually need to function?

To find out, I did a simple self-test. I called it the **Three-Click Test**.

The rule is simple: For one hour, I am only allowed to use my phone for three specific interactions. Three clicks. Three touches. After that, the phone goes in a drawer.

Here is what I chose, and what it revealed.

### 1. The Click for Safety
My first click was to check the time and look at the calendar.

This wasn’t anxiety, exactly. It was orientation. In a life where we move from task to task with such speed, we often lose our footing in *when* we are. We forget where we are in the sequence of our own day. By checking the calendar, I wasn’t procrastinating; I was anchoring myself. I needed to know what was next so I could stop worrying about what was last.

**The Reveal:** I am dependent on **structure**. Not the rigid kind, but the gentle kind. Without a clear next step, my mind starts to spin, trying to predict the future to make it feel safe.

### 2. The Click for Connection
My second click was to text a friend. Not to ask for help, not to share news. Just to send a meme.

This was the hardest one to justify. Did I *need* to send it? No. But I felt a hollow space in my chest that only seemed to fill when I saw a familiar face in my notification bar. It was a low-stakes check-in. It was a way of saying, *I am here, and you are there, and we are both okay.*

**The Reveal:** I am dependent on **micro-validation**. I don’t need a deep conversation right now. I need a digital handshake. It’s a tiny thread that keeps me tethered to the human race when the quiet of my apartment feels too much like isolation.

### 3. The Click for Escape
My third click was to open a map and look at a city I’ve never been to.

This one surprised me. I didn’t book a flight. I didn’t plan a trip. I just zoomed in on a street in Kyoto, looked at the grid of the alleys, and imagined walking them. It was a mental vacation. A way to step outside my immediate physical reality for thirty seconds.

**The Reveal:** I am dependent on **possibility**. My daily life can feel static, a loop of the same four walls and the same tasks. Looking at the map isn’t about travel; it’s about remembering that the world is bigger than my current moment. It’s a reminder that I am not stuck.

### The Honest Takeaway

When the hour was up and I put the phone away, I didn’t feel deprived. I felt… settled.

The Three-Click Test didn’t reveal that I’m addicted to my phone. It revealed that I’m dependent on **certainty, connection, and context**.

We often think our dependencies are the apps themselves: Instagram, Email, Maps. But the apps are just the vessels. The dependency is the human need underneath them.

*   I don’t need the calendar app; I need to know I’m on track.
*   I don’t need the text thread; I need to know I’m not alone.
*   I don’t need the map; I need to know there is a way out.

If you’re feeling overwhelmed by your screen time, maybe try the test. Pick your three clicks. See what you’re really reaching for.

You might find that what you’re hungry for isn’t more content. It’s just a little bit more peace.

prompt: You just ran the first batch of a summer program that funded a handful of very young first-time founders. Write a reflective essay on what the experiment taught you about young founders, how they work, and what that suggests for the future.
response:
The air in the conference room didn’t smell like coffee and ambition; it smelled like dry-erase markers and anxiety. For the first time in my career, I wasn’t looking at resumes with five years of experience or pivots that had happened three times before. I was looking at twelve-year-olds with pocket protectors and a terrifying amount of free time.

We called it a "summer bootcamp" to keep the legal teams calm, but in reality, it was a controlled experiment in radical early-stage entrepreneurship. We funded a handful of first-time founders, all under the age of fourteen, with a modest seed amount and a single constraint: build something, sell it, and show us the numbers by August 1st.

I expected chaos. I expected a struggle against the legal age of contracting. I expected them to get distracted by video games or argue about who got the better desk. What I didn’t expect was how quickly the "founder identity" collapsed and rebuilt itself around something far more primitive: curiosity.

### The Myth of the "Visionary"

The biggest lesson wasn’t about what they built. It was about *how* they decided what to build.

In the adult world of startups, the first month is often spent on "visioning." We talk about market size, TAM (Total Addressable Market), and long-term narratives. We spend weeks debating whether we are solving a problem for "Gen Z" or "SMBs."

The kids didn’t do that. They didn’t have the vocabulary for it, but more importantly, they didn’t have the ego to protect it.

One team, three girls from a suburb outside Chicago, spent the first two days trying to build an app that organized school clubs. It was a standard idea. Boring, even. But on day three, the youngest member, a girl named Maya, noticed that her friends weren’t using the app because they didn’t want to *organize* the clubs; they wanted to know who was going to the party on Friday.

They scrapped the organizational backend. They rebuilt the front end in 48 hours to be a simple, anonymous "who’s going" list. They didn’t talk about "user retention metrics" or "engagement loops." They just looked at their friends and asked, "Does this feel right?"

This taught me that young founders operate on a feedback loop that is almost embarrassingly direct. They don’t build for investors. They don’t build for the press. They build for the immediate, tangible reaction of the people around them. When the "yes" is loud, they keep going. When the "yes" is silent, they stop. There is no strategic moat to protect. There is only the mirror.

### The Absence of Fear

Working with early-stage founders is usually a negotiation with fear. Fear of running out of money. Fear of looking stupid in front of a VC. Fear that the code won’t scale.

The kids were terrified, but their fear was different. They were afraid of being wrong. They were afraid of wasting time. But they weren’t afraid of failure, because in their current life, failure is a daily, low-stakes occurrence. You miss a catch in baseball. You get a C on a math quiz. You say the wrong thing to a friend. You reset.

I watched a team of two boys, one a coder and one a designer, completely break their prototype on a Thursday night. The server crashed. The database corrupted. In any adult startup, this is a crisis. It’s a "post-mortem" waiting to happen. It’s a moment where the CEO has to step in and reassure the team that "we have a plan B."

The boys just looked at each other. "Okay," the coder said. "We’re starting over."

They didn’t panic. They didn’t blame the infrastructure. They didn’t email the board. They just reset. By Friday afternoon, they had a clunkier, slower version of the product, but it worked. They had lost nothing but a few hours, and they gained a profound resilience that no amount of MBA case studies can teach. They had learned that the machine can break, and that breaking the machine is not the end of the work; it is the work.

### The Collaborative Default

Perhaps the most surprising observation was the total absence of the "lone genius" archetype.

Adult founders often struggle with delegation. They hold onto the code, the design, and the strategy because they believe their specific brain is the bottleneck. The kids had no such hierarchy.

A twelve-year-old can’t write a backend in Python and design a UI in Figma simultaneously. So they didn’t try. They divided labor based on interest, not title. If you liked the colors, you did the colors. If you liked the logic, you did the logic. If you were bored, you swapped.

This fluidity was staggering. There was no "I’m the CEO, so I get the final say." There was only "Does this make sense to the other person?" It was pure, unadulterated peer review. They didn’t have the social capital to be stubborn. They had the social capital to be helpful.

This suggests a future where the "founder" is not a person, but a dynamic. The role of the leader is not to command, but to curate the environment where the best ideas can flow from whoever is holding the pen.

### What This Means for the Future

If we extrapolate from this small batch, the future of entrepreneurship may look less like a ladder and more like a swarm.

We are currently training founders to be CEOs. We teach them negotiation, fundraising, and public speaking. But we are failing to teach them the most important skill: the ability to kill their own baby idea without grief.

The kids did it effortlessly. They killed the club organizer app because it wasn’t fun. They killed the first version of the party list because it was slow. They weren’t attached to the *product*; they were attached to the *problem*.

This suggests a shift in how we should evaluate early-stage talent. We should stop looking for the "visionary" who has a five-year plan. We should look for the "iterator" who can pivot in 48 hours. We should stop asking young people, "Where do you see yourself in five years?" and start asking, "What did you build last weekend, and who told you to stop?"

The experiment ended in August. The kids went back to school. Some of the projects died, as most do. But a few are still alive, maintained by these same kids, now with a few more years of experience under their belts.

But the real lesson wasn’t in the products. It was in the posture.

We spend a lot of energy trying to make founders "stronger," "smarter," and "more resilient." But what I saw in that room was something simpler. They were free. Free from the weight of a career. Free from the need to be right. Free to be wrong, again and again, until the thing clicked.

Maybe the secret to the next generation of innovation isn’t better funding or better mentorship. Maybe it’s just giving them permission to be beginners. Because the best founders aren’t the ones who know the way. They’re the ones who aren’t afraid to get lost.

prompt: You're running a summer program that funds very young startup founders, and you're reading through a couple hundred applications. A lot of them come from obviously capable people pitching weak ideas. Write an essay about why smart, technically talented people so often start with bad business ideas, drawing on your own first failed startup.
response:
The inbox is a graveyard of brilliance.

For the past three weeks, I have read roughly two hundred applications for our summer accelerator. The candidates are, without exception, impressive. These are people who have already published papers, won national coding competitions, or built open-source libraries with thousands of stars. Their resumes read like who’s-who of early technical aptitude. And yet, when you peel back the layers of their pitch decks, the actual businesses they are proposing are often bafflingly weak.

It is a paradox that haunts every founder who has ever failed: the more technically competent you are, the more likely you are to build something no one wants.

I know this because I did it. My first startup, a venture I fondly remember as "The Algorithm," was a masterpiece of engineering and a disaster of market fit. We were building a "smart" photo backup system that used computer vision to tag images not just by location and date, but by sentiment. We wanted to distinguish between a picture of a birthday cake that made you happy and a picture of a birthday cake that made you anxious. It was elegant. It was sophisticated. It was, as it turned out, completely unnecessary.

When I read through these applications now, I see my own ghost in every proposal that prioritizes the novelty of the solution over the magnitude of the problem. Why does this happen? Why do the brightest minds so consistently stumble into the same trap?

First, there is the seduction of the "cool" problem. Technical talent is rare; market insight is scarce but learnable. When you are a prodigy at eighteen, your identity is wrapped up in your intellect. You solve hard problems because it validates your identity. A business idea that feels like a math puzzle is safe. It feels like *you*. A business idea that requires you to spend six months talking to frustrated middle managers about their inefficient invoicing workflows feels like selling. It feels mundane. It feels like you could be anyone.

So, we choose the hard problem that has no customer. We build the quantum-encrypted social network for hermit programmers. We build the AI that predicts the exact moment a cat will yawn. These ideas are intellectually stimulating. They are also dead on arrival because they solve problems that either don’t exist, aren’t painful enough to warrant a subscription, or are solved just fine by a simple spreadsheet.

Second, there is a fundamental misunderstanding of leverage. Young, talented founders often believe that if they can just make the technology *good enough*, the market will follow. They view the product as a closed system: input data, process through algorithm, output value. They forget that a business is an open system that lives in the messy, irrational world of human behavior.

In my first startup, we spent four months perfecting our sentiment analysis model. We hit 94% accuracy on our test sets. We were thrilled. Then we launched. We got three users. Two were my friends. One was a bot.

We had built a Ferrari engine and put it in a shopping cart. The engine was brilliant. The cart couldn’t move. The technical talent was a distraction from the core truth of business: you don’t get paid for how smart your code is; you get paid for how much pain you remove from someone else’s life. If the pain is minor, no amount of engineering genius can justify the cost of adoption.

Finally, there is the lack of scar tissue. To have a good business idea, you often need to have lived the problem. You need to have been the angry customer who screamed at a support line. You need to have been the small business owner who lost sleep over inventory counts. These are not "technical" problems. They are human problems. They are messy, unglamorous, and resistant to clean abstraction.

Young, technically gifted founders often haven’t had time to accumulate these frustrations yet. They are still in the phase of life where the world is a series of solvable equations. They haven’t met the customer yet. They haven’t sat across the table from someone and realized that the customer’s "biggest problem" is often a symptom of a different, deeper issue. They haven’t learned that the best business ideas are usually boring. They are usually a 10% improvement in a massive, existing workflow. They are unsexy. They don’t make for a great demo at a tech conference. But they scale.

So, when I close out my laptop at midnight after reviewing the hundred-and-fiftieth application, I don’t look for the smartest coder. I look for the person who sounds annoyed. I look for the person who is pitching a solution to a problem they clearly hate dealing with. I look for the founder who is less interested in the elegance of the backend and more interested in why the user is still clicking that button three times.

The world is full of people who can build anything. It is starving for people who know what to build.

My first startup failed because I was in love with the solution. My second succeeded because I was in love with the problem. The applications that make it to the next round are rarely the ones with the most impressive tech stack. They are the ones where the founder’s eyes light up not when they talk about the API, but when they talk about the customer.

prompt: I keep seeing projects claim huge speedups over established software, and when I dig in the numbers don't hold up. Write an essay about how coding agents are changing the trustworthiness of performance benchmarks. Use an example of your own if you have one, and say what, if anything, is real underneath the hype.
response:
The architecture of modern software development is undergoing a quiet but fundamental shift, driven not by new hardware, but by the proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM) coding agents. We are witnessing the erosion of the "human bottleneck" in code generation, and with it, the collapse of the traditional heuristic that "if it’s complex, it’s slow, and if it’s fast, it’s hacky." Coding agents have decoupled the cost of writing code from the cost of optimizing it, fundamentally altering the trustworthiness of performance benchmarks.

For decades, performance claims in software engineering were bound by the effort required to implement them. If a new algorithm promised a 10x speedup over a library like NumPy or Pandas, the implicit trust in that claim was high because the developer had to spend significant time wrestling with memory layouts, vectorization, and cache coherence. The complexity of the code served as a proxy for the rigor of the optimization. Today, an LLM can generate the equivalent of a week of human optimization effort in seconds. This has created a "noise floor" where performance claims are no longer correlated with engineering rigor, but with the ability to prompt a model to find a specific niche where a general-purpose library is inefficient.

Consider a common scenario in data processing: a project claims a 50% speedup over Pandas for a specific `groupby` aggregation task. Under the old paradigm, this would require a C++ backend, careful handling of NaNs, and complex memory management. A skeptical engineer would assume the new tool was doing something clever, like pre-allocation or avoiding intermediate DataFrames. But in the LLM era, the "optimization" is often trivial and brittle. The agent might have simply converted the code to use PyArrow under the hood, or hardcoded a specific data type, or, most dangerously, used `numba`’s `@njit` decorator without handling edge cases. The benchmark looks spectacular on the test data, but the trustworthiness is zero because the "optimization" is a byproduct of the model’s tendency to pick the most aggressive, least safe tool in its vocabulary, not a result of deep systems understanding.

This phenomenon creates a specific type of benchmark failure: the **Niche-Overfitting Trap**. Coding agents are excellent at pattern matching. They look at a benchmark query and generate code that solves *that* query, not the class of problems it belongs to. A new vector database might claim faster query times than PostgreSQL. A human engineer might have implemented a custom index. An LLM, however, might generate a solution that bypasses the database engine entirely for the test case, or uses a specific SQL hint that works for the sample data but degrades performance on real-world distributions. The benchmark is "real" in that the code ran fast, but it is "fake" in that it does not represent a generalizable performance improvement. The trustworthiness is compromised because the optimization is not structural; it is syntactic.

However, it would be a mistake to dismiss all performance gains as hype. There is a layer of reality beneath the noise. Coding agents are exceptionally good at **eliminating accidental complexity**. Much of the slowness in legacy codebases is not due to algorithmic inefficiency, but due to redundant data copies, unnecessary serialization, and verbose API calls. An LLM, acting as an aggressive refactorer, can strip away these layers with a consistency and speed that human developers, bound by cognitive load and fear of refactoring, often avoid.

For example, consider a Python service that is I/O bound but appears CPU bound due to excessive object instantiation. A human developer might hesitate to refactor a core class due to the risk of breaking downstream dependencies. An LLM, however, can propose a refactor that uses `slots` or dataclasses with frozen fields, or switches from JSON to MessagePack, purely based on pattern recognition of the data structure. If the benchmark shows a 20% speedup, it is likely real and robust, because the change is semantically safe and broadly applicable. The "hype" is in the magnitude of the claim (often inflated by cherry-picked microbenchmarks), but the underlying improvement in code hygiene is genuine.

The shift in trustworthiness requires a new standard for verification. We can no longer trust the code’s elegance or complexity as a signal of correctness. We must trust the **failure modes**. A trustworthy performance claim in the age of coding agents is one that includes a stress test against adversarial data, not just the happy path. If the new tool is 10x faster but crashes on a specific Unicode character or a null value that the LLM didn’t account for, the speedup is irrelevant.

Ultimately, coding agents have made performance optimization cheap, which has made it noisy. The "real" gains are those that survive the transition from the agent’s sandbox to the production environment. The "fake" gains are those that rely on the agent’s inability to model the long-tail distribution of real-world data. As we move forward, the most valuable skill for software engineers will not be writing faster code, but knowing when to doubt the speed of code that was written too quickly. The benchmark is no longer a proof of engineering; it is merely a sample from a probabilistic distribution of possibilities.

prompt: Write an essay about what goes wrong when we chase intermediate measurements instead of the thing we actually care about. Pull examples from a few very different fields, including at least one from software engineering, and be concrete about how the proxy and the goal come apart in each.
response:
We live in an age of optimization. In a complex world, the ultimate goal—happiness, health, truth, or profit—is often too vague, subjective, or slow to measure to be useful for day-to-day decision-making. To make progress, we create proxies: intermediate metrics that are supposed to track the real objective. We assume that if we maximize the proxy, we will inevitably maximize the goal.

This assumption is the root of a pervasive cognitive error known as Goodhart’s Law: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." The danger is not that the proxy is useless, but that it is *fragile*. Once we chase the proxy with enough intensity, we exploit the specific gap between the metric and the reality it was meant to represent. The proxy and the goal do not just diverge; they often invert.

To understand this failure mode, we must look at how the mechanism of measurement distorts behavior in disparate fields, from the code that runs our banks to the classrooms where we raise our children.

### Software Engineering: The Velocity Trap

In modern software development, particularly within Agile and DevOps frameworks, a popular intermediate metric is "deployment frequency" or "change velocity." The logic is sound on the surface: if we deploy code to production more often, our feedback loop is tighter, our bugs are smaller, and our risk per release is lower. The goal is **system reliability and value delivery**. The proxy is **how many times we push to the main branch per week**.

The divergence happens when the metric becomes the target. When engineering managers are judged by velocity, developers are incentivized to make changes that are *countable* but *valueless*. A developer might break a single large, complex feature into ten trivial commits just to inflate the deployment counter. Or, more dangerously, they may start bypassing quality gates to keep the flow moving.

The goal and proxy come apart when the system’s complexity exceeds its test coverage. If you deploy a change every hour, but each change is a 100-line patch to a core database schema, you haven’t reduced risk; you’ve increased the surface area for catastrophic failure. I have seen teams where "green" build status became the only truth. Developers would write code that passed the existing unit tests (the proxy) but failed in integration (the goal), because the tests were written to prove the code *could* work, not to prove it *did* work in the wild. The metric went up. The production outage rate went up. We had optimized the act of shipping, not the act of solving problems.

### Public Health: The BMI Standard

In medicine, we desperately want a quick, non-invasive way to assess metabolic health. The goal is **low risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes**. The proxy is **Body Mass Index (BMI)**, a ratio of weight to height squared.

For a long time, BMI was a reasonable heuristic. It correlated well enough with health outcomes to be useful for population-level statistics. But the moment it became the individual diagnostic target, the proxy and the goal fractured. BMI cannot distinguish between muscle mass and fat mass. It cannot distinguish between visceral fat (dangerous, wrapping around organs) and subcutaneous fat (less dangerous).

The divergence is concrete: a professional bodybuilder may have a BMI of 35 (classified as "obese") but have excellent cardiovascular health, low blood pressure, and high insulin sensitivity. Conversely, a "skinny fat" individual may have a BMI of 22 (classified as "normal") but have high visceral fat, high triglycerides, and a significantly elevated risk of a heart attack.

When doctors and patients chase the BMI number, they ignore the actual physiological signals. A patient might starve themselves to drop from a BMI of 26 to 22, losing healthy muscle and metabolic rate, while their blood lipid profile remains terrible. We chased the number on the scale and lost the health of the body. The proxy was a coarse map of the territory; by walking the map instead of the terrain, we got lost.

### Education: The Grade Inflation Spiral

In academia, the ultimate goal of education is **mastery and critical thinking**. The intermediate metric is **grades** (or standardized test scores), which are supposed to certify that mastery has occurred.

When institutions and students begin to optimize for grades rather than learning, the system decays. The proxy becomes the product. Students study for the test, not the subject. They learn to reverse-engineer what the professor wants to see in the essay, rather than engaging with the text. The metric (the "A") becomes the end state, while the goal (understanding) becomes an optional side effect.

This divergence is visible in the phenomenon of "grade inflation." As the metric (the A) becomes more common and less discriminating, it loses its signal value. Employers can no longer distinguish between a student who struggled to pass and one who dominated the course because both hold a 3.9 GPA. To regain discrimination, institutions introduce new proxies (honors, distinctions, class rank), which are then gamed in turn. The result is a system where students are trained to be test-takers, not thinkers. The proxy (the grade) has successfully measured the ability to perform in the grading system, but it has failed to measure the ability to think. The goal has been abandoned in favor of the artifact.

### The Common Thread

In all three cases, the failure follows the same trajectory:

1.  **Selection:** A proxy is chosen because it is easier to measure than the goal.
2.  **Optimization:** Agents (developers, patients, students) adjust their behavior to maximize the proxy.
3.  **Exploitation:** Agents find the "loophole"—the way to increase the metric without improving the underlying reality.
4.  **Divergence:** The metric continues to rise (or stay flat), but the goal stagnates or degrades.

The core issue is that **proxies are local approximations**. They work only within a certain range of behavior. Once you push the system to the edge of that range—by optimizing relentlessly—the approximation breaks.

The lesson is not to abandon metrics. We cannot manage what we cannot measure. The lesson is to treat metrics as **diagnostic tools**, not **steering wheels**. We should monitor velocity, BMI, and grades to detect when something is wrong, but we must never let them dictate what is right. If we chase the tail of the dog, we will run in circles, getting winded while the dog keeps walking forward. We must keep our eyes on the destination, even when the GPS signal is weak.

prompt: Paul Graham recently wrote that convertible notes and rolling closes are replacing fixed-valuation equity rounds put together by angel syndicates. I'm a programmer and that sentence is Greek to me. Can you explain it all for a layman: what angels are, why raising from them is painful, what valuation means, and how convertible notes, discounts and valuation caps work? Use simple made-up numbers.
response:
Here is the breakdown of that financial sentence, translated from "Venture Capital" into plain English.

### 1. Who are the Angels?
An "angel investor" is a wealthy individual who uses their own money to invest in very early-stage companies (startups).

In the old days, you could go to a single rich person, show them your idea, and say, "Give me $100,000 for 10% of my company." They would sign a check, and it was done.

**Why it is painful:**
Paul Graham says this is no longer the norm. Now, startups rarely raise from one person. They raise from a "syndicate" (a group).
*   **The Negotiation Hell:** You don't just ask for money. You have to sit in a room with 5–10 different wealthy people. Each one has different terms. One wants a board seat. Another wants to be the first to know if you fire your CTO. Another wants a right to veto hiring decisions.
*   **The Time Sink:** You are spending weeks doing legal work, answering due diligence questions, and negotiating terms with humans who are not customers. You are not coding; you are doing HR and legal work for your investors.

### 2. What is a Valuation?
A valuation is the price tag you put on your entire company.

**The Simple Math:**
If you say your startup is worth **$10 million**, and you want to raise **$2 million** in new money:
*   Total company value after the raise = $12 million.
*   The investors get $2 million / $12 million = **~16.6% of the company.**

**The Pain Point:**
To get that 16.6%, you had to agree *right now* that your company is worth $10 million. But your startup is just an idea and a prototype. You don't have revenue. How do you know it's worth $10 million?
*   The investors say, "It's only worth $5 million."
*   You say, "It's worth $20 million."
*   You argue for three weeks. This is the "fixed-valuation round." It is painful because you are gambling on a number that is basically a guess, and you are fighting over it.

### 3. The New Way: Convertible Notes
To avoid the pain of arguing over the $10 million price tag, most startups now use a **Convertible Note**.

A convertible note is **not** an investment in shares yet. It is a **loan** with a twist: it turns into equity (shares) later.

**How it works:**
1.  You say, "I will take $2 million from you now."
2.  The investors say, "Okay. But we don't want to agree on what the company is worth *today*. We will wait until you do a 'real' round of funding (usually called a Series A) where you have real revenue and big firms are writing checks. We will figure out the percentage then."
3.  You sign a promissory note. You get the cash. No percentage is agreed upon yet.

This skips the painful valuation negotiation. You get the money fast.

### 4. The "Twist": Caps and Discounts
If the loan just converts at whatever price is set in the future, the early investors are taking a huge risk. They are giving you money when you are risky. To protect themselves, they add two mechanisms:

#### A. The Valuation Cap
This is a safety net for the investor. It says: "No matter how high your company is valued in the next round, we will calculate our shares as if the company was worth only $X."

**Let's use made-up numbers:**
*   You raise $2 million now on a convertible note.
*   You agree on a **Valuation Cap of $10 million**.
*   One year later, you do a Series A round. A big firm values your company at **$40 million** (because you did great!).
*   The big firm pays $40 million for 25% of the company.
*   **Without a cap:** Your early investors' $2 million would convert at the $40 million valuation. They would get very few shares.
*   **With the $10 million cap:** The law says, "For the early investors, pretend the company was only worth $10 million when they bought in."
    *   $2 million invested into a $10 million cap = they get **20% of the company**.
    *   Even though the company is now worth $40 million, they keep those 20% shares. They just got a huge free ride.

#### B. The Discount
This is a bonus for the early investors. It says: "We will buy our shares at a 20% discount compared to the new investors."

**Using the same numbers:**
*   The Series A price is $40 million.
*   The early investors get a **20% discount**.
*   So, they get to buy their shares at $32 million (80% of $40 million).
*   This means they get more shares for the same $2 million than the new Series A investors get.

### Summary: Why is this replacing fixed rounds?

**Old Way (Fixed Valuation):**
*   You argue for 3 months about whether the company is worth $5M or $10M.
*   You sign a term sheet.
*   You do 40 hours of legal work.
*   You get the money.
*   *Result:* You spent 3 months not building your product.

**New Way (Convertible Note):**
*   You say, "I'll take $2M with a $10M cap and 20% discount."
*   You sign a simple 10-page document.
*   You get the money in 2 weeks.
*   You build your product for a year.
*   When you do the real round, the note automatically converts into shares.
*   *Result:* You saved 3 months of legal/argument time.

**The Trade-off:**
It is faster and less painful for the startup, but it is more expensive in the long run. The "cap" and "discount" guarantee that the early investors will get a much bigger slice of the pie than the later investors, even if the company becomes a massive success. You are paying for speed.

prompt: Some developers commenting on my last post said they don't want non-technical 'idiots' using their software anyway. I'd like to answer that. Write an essay about why customers won't ask the 'stupid' questions they have, what that costs a software seller, and what to do about it. A personal story would help.
response:
The comment section of a developer’s post is rarely a safe space for nuance, but it is a window into a specific, dangerous mindset. When a developer dismisses non-technical users as "idiots" who shouldn’t be using the software, they are revealing a fundamental misunderstanding of their own business model. They are confusing "user" with "operator."

The assumption behind the "idiot" comment is that the product is a tool, and tools require training. A wrench doesn’t care if you don’t know what a hex bolt is; you just turn it. But software is not a wrench. Software is an interface to a system of logic. When a developer builds a tool that requires the user to understand the underlying architecture to function correctly, they haven’t built a product; they’ve built a dependency.

The most immediate cost of this dependency is the silence of the customer. There is a specific silence that follows the moment a user realizes they are being judged by the machine. It is not the silence of contentment; it is the silence of shame.

Consider a story from my own past. I once managed the rollout of a new inventory management system for a mid-sized retail chain. The software was elegant, built by engineers who were proud of its modular design. It required the user to understand "stock levels" versus "order quantities" versus "buffer thresholds." To the developers, this was clear. To the store managers, who were often part-time and had no tech background, it was a wall of jargon.

In the first month, we had zero support tickets. The developers were thrilled. "Look," they said, "we don’t need a help desk. The UI is intuitive."

Then came the quarterly audit. The numbers were wrong. Inventory was reported as higher than it was, leading to over-ordering that tied up cash flow for weeks. When we dug into the logs, we didn’t find bugs. We found patterns of avoidance.

One store manager, a woman named Elena who had worked at the store for twelve years, told me what had happened. She didn’t know what a "buffer threshold" was. She knew that if she entered a number that seemed too high, the system would flag it as an "anomaly" in red text. She didn’t know if it was wrong, so she stopped entering it. She just left the field blank. The system, designed to be "intuitive," interpreted the blank as "zero."

Elena didn’t ask a "stupid" question. She didn’t call support and say, "I don’t understand buffer thresholds." She made a quiet, rational decision to stop interacting with the part of the software she feared would judge her. She preserved her dignity by preserving her ignorance. And in doing so, she broke the business logic.

This is the true cost of the "idiot" mindset. It is not that customers ask stupid questions; it is that they stop asking questions at all. They stop reporting edge cases. They stop telling you that the button in the bottom left corner feels like it might delete their database. They stop telling you that the error message says "Error 402: Insufficient Funds" when they have plenty of funds, because that message makes them feel stupid for not understanding finance.

When you treat users as idiots, you train them to be silent. And silent users are expensive users.

The cost is threefold. First, there is the direct financial loss of broken workflows, like Elena’s inventory error. Second, there is the loss of feedback. Developers love feedback, but they only like feedback that validates their assumptions. They don’t want to know that the "intuitive" flow actually causes users to click three times in a panic. They want to be told the code is clean. So, the users stop sending the ugly, messy, human feedback that actually improves the product.

Third, and most insidiously, there is the loss of trust. Trust is the currency of software. When a user feels that the software is designed for someone smarter than them, they stop trusting the output. If they don’t trust the output, they don’t rely on the product. They use spreadsheets. They use sticky notes. They use the old system. They churn.

So, what do we do about it?

We have to accept that the "stupid" question is the most valuable data point in the room. If a user asks, "Why does this button do that?" the answer is not "Read the documentation." The answer is, "You are right, this button is confusing. I will fix it."

Designers and developers need to shift their metric from "feature completeness" to "friction reduction." The goal is not to make the software so complex that only experts can use it, but to make the software so forgiving that a beginner can use it without fear.

This means designing for the "Elena." It means assuming the user will make a mistake, not because they are stupid, but because they are human. It means providing clear, non-judgmental error messages. It means offering a "undo" button for everything. It means writing documentation that speaks in the language of the user’s job, not the developer’s language.

When a developer says they don’t want non-technical people using their software, they are saying they don’t want to be accountable for the user experience. They are saying, "My code works; your problem is your brain."

But software is not just code. Software is a relationship. And in any relationship, if one party refuses to meet the other halfway, the relationship ends. The customers won’t ask the stupid questions. They will just leave. And when they leave, they won’t tell you why. They will just stop using your product, and you will never know that you lost them because you thought they were idiots.

prompt: Why do deep neural networks work so well? I'd like a blog post that tries to answer this through the lens of natural language processing results, aimed at readers who know some machine learning but haven't followed NLP research closely.
response:
